r4_y1.text: He backs up until the counter stops him. His hands come up, open, the way you would calm a frightened animal. “Okay,” he says. “Okay.” Over his shoulder, on the stairs, a small face is watching. Your child is watching you, not him.

choices.label: Leave the house until you can breathe

r4_y2.text: He flinches before you have done anything. That is what you will remember later: the flinch. He scoops the child up from the stairs, grabs his phone from the table, and backs toward the front door without taking his eyes off you.

choices.label: Let them go

“I need help. I don’t know how to stop.”

r4_end_apart.text: He goes quiet on the other side of the door. Nothing has been settled, but the shouting has stopped, for now.

r4_end_cooloff.text: He goes quiet. Neither of you has won, but it stopped. Now you have to decide what you will say in the morning.

r4_end_walkout.text: You close the front door quietly behind you. The night air is cool. You don’t know where you will go yet, only that you don’t want to be in that room.

r4_end_help.text: A voice on the line asks if you are safe. It is the first sensible question anyone has asked tonight.

r4_end_leave.text: You are halfway down the street before you notice you are not wearing shoes. A neighbour’s porch light comes on. You keep walking towards it.

r4_end_freeze.text: Time stretches. Afterwards nothing in the house is where it was. Freezing is not a failure. It is what many people’s bodies do.

r4_end_neighbour.text: A knock at the door, then another, firmer. A neighbour’s voice: “Is everything all right?” The house goes quiet. You do not have to explain anything yet.

r4_end_sister.text: Your phone rings eleven seconds later. You let it ring out loud, on purpose. He steps away from the counter, and your sister’s voice fills the kitchen.

r4_end_shame.text: You sit with your back against the cupboard until your hands stop shaking. He doesn’t come closer, and you don’t ask him to. Saying sorry is the start of something. It is not the same as it never having happened.

r4_end_cooldown.text: You walk until the streetlights change from orange to white. Tonight you were the one who frightened someone. Admitting that to yourself is the first useful thing you have done all evening.

r4_end_theyleave.text: The car pulls away with both of them in it. The house is very quiet now, and every room still has your voice in it.

r4_end_bluelights.text: He doesn’t fight you for the door. He carries the child into the bathroom and locks it, and you hear him on the phone. When the officers arrive, they speak to you outside on the step, for a long time.

r4_end_askhelp.text: He doesn’t put the child down, and he doesn’t leave either. He finds a number on his phone, holds it out at arm’s length, and lets you be the one to press call.

r4_s3c.text: Above you, a floorboard creaks. Both of you look up at the same moment. For a second you are not on opposite sides of the kitchen. You are two parents listening for a child.

r4_end_tin.text: The tin is lighter than you remember, and heavier. It is not much. It is enough for a taxi and two nights somewhere quiet. You counted it so many times that your hands know the way out.

r4_end_proof.text: The photo sends with a small sound. Ten seconds later your sister replies: “I’m calling the police. Stay where you are safe.” For the first time tonight, it is not only your word.

r4_end_stairs.text: Your child is sitting on the top step, knees pulled up. You sit on either side of them. Nobody says sorry yet, but nobody goes back downstairs to finish the fight either.

r4_end_counsel.text: He finds the number on the fridge, the one you both pretended not to see. “Monday,” he says. It is not peace. It is a time and a place to fight fairly, with someone watching.
